root.name: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Rubinstein System
root.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Bb4 4. e3

sources.title: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Play, Attack, and Counter as White & Black

Nimzo-Indian Defense - Must-Know Structures in the Rubinstein Variation (search extract only, page not opened)

overview: White ignores the pin and the threat of ...Bxc3+ and develops with Bd3, Nf3, O-O (or Ne2), accepting that doubled c-pawns may arise and banking on the bishop pair and central space; the e4 square is the recurring battleground. Black chooses between 4...O-O (flexible; 5.Bd3 d5 6.Nf3 c5 is the main line), 4...c5 (immediate pressure on d4; Hübner-style 5.Ne2 lines where White avoids doubled pawns) and 4...b6 (St. Petersburg, controlling e4 with ...Bb7). Typical middlegames feature central tension and a pawn-structure battle: hanging pawns on c3/d4 which Black blockades with knights on c4/d5, an isolated d4-pawn for White after ...cxd4 exd4, or a closed knight-versus-bishops game in the Hübner. Play is positional and manoeuvring, with understanding of the structures more important than memorised sequences.

white_ideas.idea: Develop first and settle the centre later: Bd3 to fight for e4 and eye the kingside, then Nf3 and O-O.
Accept doubled c-pawns after ...Bxc3+ bxc3 in return for the bishop pair, central space and the half-open b-file.
Nge2 (5.Nge2 or Hübner 5.Ne2) to recapture on c3 with the knight and keep the pawn structure intact, at the cost of blocking the f1-bishop.
With an isolated d4-pawn, either play for the initiative and a kingside attack or prepare d4-d5 to dissolve it.
Hold the centre with d4 and e3 and aim for a slow edge from the bishop pair.

black_ideas.idea: Pin c3 and restrain e4, then choose the central break: ...c5 and/or ...d5.
4...c5 to challenge d4 directly; White typically avoids recapturing with the b-pawn after ...Bxc3 here because of the risk of tripled c-pawns.
...b6 and ...Bb7 (or ...Ba6) to control e4 and the long diagonal; the b7-bishop becomes very strong in the middlegame.
Blockade White's hanging pawns on c3/d4 with knights on c4 and d5, queen to c7, rooks to the c- or d-files.
Against an isolated d4-pawn, fianchetto the bishop to b7 (Karpov-style ...b6) and play on the queenside majority or via ...Na5-c4.
Hübner: trade ...Bxc3 voluntarily, close the position with ...d6 and ...e5 and use knights against White's doubled pawns.

typical_structures.structure: Hanging pawns on c3 and d4 (after ...Bxc3 bxc3 and ...dxc4 Bxc4), targets for Black's blockading knights.
Isolated queen's pawn on d4 after ...c5, ...d5, ...dxc4 and ...cxd4 exd4; piece activity versus a long-term weakness.
Doubled c-pawns for White after ...Bxc3+ bxc3; 'not always bad' for White as they give space and open lines, but weak if blockaded.
Hübner-style closed centre: White's e3/d4/c4 against Black's d6/e5, with the knight-versus-bishop battle.

character.notes: Chessable: solid rather than sharp, Black gets 'fine' positions in all lines (s2). Chessworld: broad practical main line, flexible development, 'more solid and flexible than 4.Qc2' (s4). Chess.com calls the Hübner a closed positional system with a strategically rich middlegame decided by manoeuvring, not tactics (s5). The 4...O-O 5.Bd3 d5 6.Nf3 c5 lines can reach IQP or hanging pawn positions with more dynamic piece play. Overall: Balanced, not Quiet as in a London, not Sharp.

gambit.notes: No material is given on purpose. Any pawn grabs (e.g. ...dxc4) are recaptured by force.

soundness.notes: Fully sound for both sides. Wikipedia: Black achieves full equality in the sound variations, and the Nimzo has been played by every world champion since Capablanca (s1). Chessiverse figures show White 49.5%, draws 5.7%, Black 44.9% over 1.97M games, and White 48.3% / draws 9.6% / Black 42.2% at 2500 Elo (s3).

structure.notes: Central tension is typical and the structure depends on Black's choice: 4...O-O/...d5/...c5 gives hanging pawns or an IQP (open, with tension, piece play); 4...b6 keeps the centre fluid; the Hübner is closed. The most-played subtree branches (Ragozin-type ...d5 after 5.Nf3, Panov-type IQP) point to a partly open centre with tension rather than a locked one. A classifier will have to pick one value for a variable structure.

approach.notes: A main line, not a set-up played against anything: it depends on the Nimzo move order 3...Bb4. Mainstream at elite level (Chessiverse lists Gligoric, Aleksandrov, Donner as White practitioners and Korchnoi, Kholmov, Matanovic as Black); top-move adherence rises from 28% at 400 Elo to 65.3% at 2500, i.e. theory matters most at the top (s3). Wikipedia: Rubinstein 4.e3 is White's most popular approach alongside 4.Qc2 (s1).

level.notes: Chessable: Black's opening moves are easy to understand and theory is easier to learn than many openings, but the variation rewards understanding of pawn structures and piece coordination (s2). Chessworld: suits players who prefer strategic plans over memorisation, though mastering central tension and structure assessment is essential (s4). Own understanding, flagged: the many structures (IQP, hanging pawns, doubled c-pawns, Hübner) each need a different plan, so the hard part is judgement, not move memory.

sublines_that_differ.name: Hübner Variation (4...c5 5.Ne2 ... 6.a3 Bxc3+ 7.Nxc3)
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Bb4 4. e3 c5 5. Ne2
sublines_that_differ.how: Closed, positional, knight-versus-bishop play; White recaptures with the knight and avoids doubled pawns. Differs from the main line's dynamic structures.

sublines_that_differ.name: St. Petersburg / ...b6 lines
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Bb4 4. e3 b6
sublines_that_differ.how: Black fianchettoes and fights for e4 with ...Bb7; central tension is maintained and the play is more flexible.

sublines_that_differ.name: Panov-type IQP lines
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Bb4 4. e3 c5 5. Nf3 cxd4 6. exd4 d5
sublines_that_differ.how: White gets an isolated d4-pawn with open files and piece activity, a structure for IQP play rather than a manoeuvring game.

sublines_that_differ.name: 4...O-O 5.Bd3 d5 6.Nf3 c5 (hanging pawns)
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Bb4 4. e3 O-O 5. Bd3 d5 6. Nf3 c5
sublines_that_differ.how: The most played main line; leads to hanging pawns or an IQP depending on the exchanges.

description.claim: The Rubinstein System is a classical, highly respected line aiming for a solid central set-up and a strategically complex game.
description.note: Named after Rubinstein; the sources describe it as solid, flexible and the practical main line. (It is White's system within the Nimzo, rather than a 'response to the Nimzo-Indian'.)

description.claim: By playing 4.e3, White prepares to recapture on c3 with the e-pawn, avoiding the doubled pawns common in other lines.
description.note: 4.e3 does not prepare an e-pawn recapture; on ...Bxc3+ White recaptures with the b-pawn (bxc3), giving doubled c-pawns, which the sources say White accepts. Doubled pawns are avoided only in the Hübner/Nge2 version, by recapturing with the knight.

description.claim: The play is a slow, manoeuvring battle.
description.note: True of the main and Hübner lines; the IQP lines are more dynamic.

common_plans.claim: White: develop with Bd3, Nf3, 0-0 and a3, aiming to use the bishop pair and central space for a long-term advantage or a kingside attack.
common_plans.note: Bd3, Nf3 and O-O are the standard development; the bishop pair and central space are cited. a3 appears to force a decision on the bishop; a kingside attack is the softer element.

common_plans.claim: Black: challenge the centre with ...c5 and/or ...d5, often trading the bishop on c3 to create structural weaknesses and counterplay against the c4-pawn.
White: in lines with ...d5, White can play cxd5 to create an isolated queen's pawn position with open files.
common_plans.note: The IQP arises from ...c5, ...d5, ...dxc4 and ...cxd4 exd4 (an isolated d4-pawn), not from cxd5, which leads to a different, symmetrical-type structure (own understanding, flagged). Sources describe the IQP via exchanges on d4 and c4.

common_plans.claim: Black: blockade White's centre after ...Bxc3 bxc3 by controlling d5 and e4 and reroute the f6-knight to support the queenside.
common_plans.note: Knight blockade on c4/d5 and control of e4 are cited; knight to c4 via a5 is cited for the IQP structure.
